title: Software Deployment Tools
summary: Software deployment tools are the enterprise's own remote execution machinery, and an intruder who obtains the right account inherits it. Configuration management, endpoint management, and deployment suites such as Microsoft Configuration Manager, Microsoft Intune, Azure Arc, AWS Systems Manager, and similar platforms exist to run commands and install software on large numbers of endpoints without any user interaction, usually with highly privileged service accounts and often in the context of the local system account. That design makes the abuse hard to separate from administration: the legitimate agent, service, port, and identity are all present, and the payload may be delivered through the tool's normal distribution channels. An attacker can use the platform for code execution, for lateral movement to every enrolled host, for reconnaissance through hardware and software inventory data, and for destructive actions such as wiping drives at scale; cloud hosted variants and CI/CD integrations extend the reach from on-premises endpoints to cloud instances and pipeline runners. Detection should focus on who used the console and what they asked it to do. Console and provider audit logs, the creation and approval of new deployment packages or scripts, service account authentications from unusual locations, agents executing content that was never signed or approved by change management, and deployment jobs that target the whole estate rather than a defined group are the practical indicators, and a baseline of normal administrative behaviour is what makes them stand out.

beginner.definition: Software deployment tools are programs that install software and run tasks on many computers at once. Administrators use them for updates and fixes. An attacker who takes over such a tool can run their own commands everywhere it manages.
beginner.whyItMatters: These systems are built to run code on many machines without asking users. That is their normal job. When an attacker controls one, the harmful action looks like a normal deployment, and a single action can reach every computer in the company.
howItWorks: Companies install management software so one team can update thousands of computers easily.
Each computer runs an agent that accepts tasks from the central management server.
The agent usually runs with very high rights, often as the local system account.
An attacker steals or creates an administrator account for the management platform.
They publish a package or script through the console, and every targeted agent runs it.
They can also use the platform to gather information about computers, or to move to other systems.
beginner.example: Think of a building with a central maintenance system. The manager can switch lights on and unlock doors from one office. If someone copies the manager's key, every floor opens for them. The workers inside only see a normal, authorised instruction.
takeaways: Management platforms run code by design, so a malicious task can look completely legitimate.
Protect administrator accounts for these tools as strongly as domain administrator accounts.
Review the platform's own audit log, because it records who created and changed each task.

objectives: Explain what configuration and software deployment platforms do in an enterprise.
Describe why their privileged agents make them valuable to an attacker.
Explain how a deployment tool can be used for both execution and lateral movement.
Identify the audit and provider logs that record deployment activity.
Describe controls that reduce the risk from a compromised management account.
